articles.title: A Brisbane man grew up across the street from a 1920s home where he played as a child; after almost pulling out of its auction, he outbid three others to buy the six-bedroom property for A$4.9 million
articles.summary: A childhood connection has turned into a multimillion-dollar property purchase in Brisbane, where a local buyer has acquired a historic Queenslander that
articles.body: A childhood connection has turned into a multimillion-dollar property purchase in Brisbane, where a local buyer has acquired a historic Queenslander that he once knew as a child. The six-bedroom residence in Newmarket sold for A$4.9 million after a competitive auction, according to reporting by The Sydney Morning Herald, Domain and Ray White. The buyer grew up across the street from the property at 11 Watson Street and had spent much of his childhood playing there. Despite his long-standing attachment to the house, he nearly missed the opportunity to own it, having told the selling agent on the morning of the auction that he no longer intended to participate. He eventually changed his mind and joined three other local bidders in the contest for the property, which sits on an expansive 1,124-square-metre block on Windsor Hill in one of Newmarket's established residential neighbourhoods. The auction attracted a crowd of nearly 60 people, with bidding beginning at A$4 million. The price climbed in increments of A$100,000 before reaching A$4.6 million, where proceedings stalled. After further negotiations, the buyer eventually secured the property for A$4.9 million. Domain's account of the sale noted that four bidders had registered, although only two actively participated in the bidding.A century-old home with a personal connectionBuilt in the 1920s, the Queenslander has retained its character while undergoing renovations over the years. The property features six bedrooms, a wine cellar, a separate teenagers' wing and expansive outdoor spaces. Its elevated position also offers sweeping views of Brisbane. The house has had relatively few owners during its century-long history. It last changed hands in 2009 for A$2.6 million, making its latest sale a considerable increase in value. The current owners decided to sell as they looked to downsize. The property also attracted attention beyond its eventual buyer because of its architectural character and location. Watson Street is regarded as one of Newmarket's sought-after residential addresses, with the property's substantial landholding adding to its appeal.A standout sale amid a subdued property marketThe A$4.9 million transaction was particularly notable given the broader conditions in Brisbane's housing market. According to Domain's auction results for the week ending November 7, 2026, the city recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 21 per cent, with 167 auctions scheduled and 122 results reported. Of these, 26 properties sold, while 76 were passed in and 20 withdrawn.The figures point to a challenging market, where buyers have become more cautious amid higher borrowing costs and uncertainty around interest rates. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver has also highlighted the weakness in Brisbane's auction performance compared with the same period last year. However, the Newmarket sale demonstrates that distinctive properties with desirable locations and established character can continue to attract substantial interest, even when overall market activity is subdued.The buyer's purchase was ultimately about more than acquiring a large family home. It brought him back to a place that had been part of his childhood, turning a familiar house across the street into a property he could finally call his own.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Olivia Wilde backed a free school in earthquake-hit Haiti that began with 300 students; the charity says it has since helped over 32,000 children, and a September 2026 fundraiser added more than $700,000
articles.summary: Hollywood actress Olivia Wilde has been associated with an initiative that has worked to make education more accessible to children in Haiti, a country
articles.body: Hollywood actress Olivia Wilde has been associated with an initiative that has worked to make education more accessible to children in Haiti, a country that has faced years of political instability, poverty and humanitarian crises. Through Artists for Peace and Justice (APJ), an organisation supporting education and community development, the effort helped establish a free school in Port-au-Prince following the devastating 2010 earthquake. According to the organisation's official website, what began as a school for 300 students has grown into a larger educational programme supporting more than 1,400 students each year. APJ also credits its wider work with helping over 32,000 children access education, healthcare and other opportunities. The connection between Wilde and the organisation goes beyond celebrity support. She is listed on APJ's official website as a member of its board of directors. She has also spoken about the importance of supporting organisations that work closely with local communities rather than relying solely on outside aid. Her association with the initiative dates back to its early years, when the organisation was expanding its education programmes in Haiti.How the school came into existenceThe Academy for Peace and Justice was established in the aftermath of the January 12, 2010 earthquake, which devastated large parts of Haiti, including its capital, Port-au-Prince. The disaster killed hundreds of thousands of people and left millions without homes, adding to the challenges faced by a country already struggling with poverty and limited access to education.Rather than restricting its response to emergency relief, APJ focused on creating an institution that could provide children with opportunities beyond primary schooling. A gathering of artists and supporters helped raise $4.5 million towards purchasing land, building the school and providing scholarships to students for their first five years.The school opened in October 2010 and was designed to serve children from disadvantaged communities. Its early student population included around 300 children between the ages of 12 and 18. The institution was also designed and developed with Haitian leadership, teachers and staff at its centre.Over the years, the six-acre campus has expanded considerably. APJ says the Academy now supports more than 1,400 students and employs approximately 180 teachers and staff annually. The organisation's wider programmes have also extended beyond traditional schooling, with support for healthcare, scholarships and vocational opportunities. Another part of its work was helping rebuild and expand Haiti's film school into the Artists Institute, a professional training centre supporting the country's film and music industries. APJ continued supporting the institute until 2018, and it is now run by Haitian staff, including former students.A fresh fundraising effort in TorontoThe organisation's work received another boost in September 2026, when its 18th annual Artists for Peace and Justice Gala raised more than $700,000 during the Toronto International Film Festival. According to NOW Toronto and a September 14 announcement from the organisation, the event was held at the Windsor Arms Hotel and recognised three prominent Canadian personalities: Actors Andrea Martin and Emily Hampshire, and musician Jann Arden.The evening brought together members of the entertainment and philanthropic communities, with George Stroumboulopoulos and Kardinal Offishall serving as co-hosts. The programme also included musical performances, an awards presentation and a live auction featuring works by artists including Russell Young, Tyler Shields and Mr. Brainwash. The latest fundraiser adds to APJ's fundraising record. The organisation says it has raised more than $37 million since its inception, helping over 32,000 students access education and healthcare.Education amid Haiti's worsening crisisThe fundraising efforts come at a particularly difficult time for Haiti, where escalating gang violence has disrupted everyday life, displaced families and made access to essential services increasingly difficult. The challenges are also affecting children's education. APJ's board chair Natasha Koifman told NOW Toronto that violence has prevented a significant number of the school's students from attending classes. The organisation is increasingly focused on ensuring that children have a way to continue their education despite the insecurity around them.The situation extends beyond schools. A September 2026 assessment supported by UNICEF, the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme estimated that 253,725 children between six months and five years of age could experience acute malnutrition in Haiti between June 2026 and May 2027. Nearly 94,000 are expected to face severe acute malnutrition.For APJ, continuing to invest in education is therefore about more than keeping classrooms open. It is also about giving children the chance to build a future in a country where violence, poverty and instability have made even ordinary opportunities increasingly difficult to access.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'No long speeches': Rahul Gandhi renews debate challenge to PM Modi with a 'guarantee'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Friday renewed his challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a one-on-one public debate, claiming that the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Friday renewed his challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a one-on-one public debate, claiming that the prime minister would not remain in office after facing him in a direct exchange.During an 'Ask Me' session on Instagram, the Congress MP was asked why he continued to insist on a public debate when the BJP had said the discussion could take place in Parliament.The leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha said he was not allowed to speak freely in the House and alleged that his microphone had been switched off."You did not let me talk on the farm bills, vote chori, SIR, China, on (Gen) Naravane's book, Epstein. I want a one-on-one debate. I don't want a debate entailing long speeches," he said.The Raebareli MP proposed a direct exchange in which both leaders could make allegations against each other, rather than deliver lengthy speeches."I want that Narendra Modi makes allegations against me and I do the same to him. He can come; there will be a table, on one side there will be Narendra Modi ji and on the other side, it would be me," he said.He added that he would have no objection if Adani Group chairperson Gautam Adani or Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat was appointed to judge the debate."But I guarantee that the prime minister will not remain the PM after a one-on-one debate with me," Rahul said.He also alleged that PM Modi is anti-national and is controlled by foreign powers.Responding to a question regarding proof of such foreign aid allegations, he said, “The proof is here. It's in this phone. The Prime Minister knows it because he taps my phone. The moment he comes for the debate, one-on-one debate, everybody will know who's controlled by foreign powers, who's an anti-national, since when he's been an anti-national, and lots of other details that I know and I wrote on my phone.”Rahul has repeatedly challenged PM Modi to debateThe Congress leader has made several public calls for PM Modi to face him in an open debate. He had earlier claimed that it would take him just five minutes to establish that the prime minister was a "traitor".In a series of posts and videos shared on X last week, Rahul also challenged PM Modi to debate allegations concerning foreign influence, national security and who was anti-national.In one video, he said 24 hours had passed since he first issued the challenge and urged the prime minister to choose any venue. He proposed that the discussion take place in front of the media and the country's youth, with both leaders seated across a table and PM Modi choosing the moderator or judge. Rahul had suggested Bhagwat for the role.In another post, former Congress president renewed the challenge while responding to PM Modi's 'Dimagi Naxal' remarks. Addressing CRPF personnel who had attended the prime minister's Diwali event in Bastar, he claimed their expressions suggested they did not agree with PM Modi's comments."Your faces said it all: you didn't buy the PM's lies. He called us Naxals," Gandhi wrote.He also said the debate should address who was anti-national and who was controlled by foreign forces.BJP dismisses challengeBJP leaders have scoffed at Rahul's repeated calls for a debate, alleging that he has avoided discussions in Parliament.Union home minister Amit Shah has challenged Rahul to debate him in Parliament, asking him to bring his allegations and arguments to the House instead of taking political debate to the streets."If you (Rahul Gandhi) wish to engage in a responsible discussion—if your concerns hold truth, substance, and logic—then come and discuss them inside Parliament. Let’s face each other head-on! But you won’t be able to handle the answers; as always, you will just run away," Shah said at a rally in Karnal, Haryana.Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman has also said that Parliament already provides a platform for such an exchange and urged the Congress MP to show "some seriousness and responsibility" in his role as the leader of the opposition.Rahul's latest remarks come amid the continuing political exchange between the Congress and the BJP over his allegations against Modi and the prime minister's criticism of the opposition.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday praised writer and RSS leader HV Sheshadri for his contribution to nation-building, saying he dedicated his life to preparing "dedicated, capable, and disciplined citizens".Speaking at the Golden Jubilee celebrations of Prashanti Kutiram at S-VYASA University in Bengaluru, PM also highlighted India's efforts to take its cultural heritage, traditional knowledge and scientific achievements to the global stage."Friends, along with the grand jubilee of Prashanti Kuttrem, this year we are celebrating the birth centenary of the revered H.V. Sheshadri. I pay my respectful homage. Sheshadri dedicated his entire life to furthering the mission of nation-building through the creation of the H.V. Seshadri Institute," PM Modi said."He knew that to take the country to the pinnacle of success it would require dedicated, capable, and disciplined citizens. Sheshadri ji devoted himself to preparing such individuals," PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also spoke about India's spiritual legacy, recalling the contribution of Swami Vivekananda in awakening the country's spiritual consciousness and introducing yoga to its youth."When the country was shackled by the chains of slavery, millions of freedom fighters were fighting for independence on one side... while on the other, there were national sages like Swami Vivekananda, who awakened India's spiritual consciousness. Showed India's youth the path of yoga. Over the past 12 years, India has confidently presented its culture, its identity, and its knowledge and science to the world. This is why the whole world now celebrates International Day of Yoga at India's initiative. Yoga asanas have also been recognized as a competitive sport in India. Events such as Khelo India and the National Games have also created new opportunities for yoga asanas. These changes are very important for India. They have also opened up opportunities for people involved. We have encouraged research related to Ayurveda and Ayurveda-based patents, and today we are seeing the results of that too. Exports of AYUSH and herbal products from India are steadily increasing," the PM said.The Golden Jubilee celebrations of Prashanti Kutiram and the birth centenary of HV Sheshadri was organised by the S-VYASA Registered Society in memory of the writer. articles.title: US plans to turn submarines into drone motherships: How India is charting its own course
articles.summary: The role of the attack submarine is being redrawn with the US Navy's next nuclear attack submarine, the SSN(X), will be faster, spend less time in repair
articles.body: The role of the attack submarine is being redrawn with the US Navy's next nuclear attack submarine, the SSN(X), will be faster, spend less time in repair and act as a mothership for a constellation of undersea drones, according to Rear Admiral Andrew Miller, the Navy's head of requirements for submarines. Speaking at the Naval Submarine League's annual conference on Thursday, he said the service is finalising its analysis of alternatives for the class that will follow the Virginia-class boats.The US Navy is looking at a hull of larger diameter, closer to the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine, with capabilities more like the Seawolf class, a late Cold War design widely seen as the most lethal attack submarine in the world. The idea is to move the submarine from a lone hunter-killer to a launch platform for uncrewed systems fired from its torpedo tubes, extending the reach of the manned fleet.Why unmanned vessels matterUnmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) and unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) were first used for scientific research and offshore inspections. They are now being developed for surveillance, mine warfare, reconnaissance, anti-submarine warfare and the protection of undersea infrastructure. They can stay deployed for long periods, work in contested waters without risking crews, and carry sonar, magnetometers and other sensors to survey sea beds, find mines and monitor cables and pipelines.India's progressIndia has been building its own capability, at the annual Swavlamban in 2023, to guide industry on systems that match its requirements and the Atmanirbhar Bharat drive. By the end of that year, the Defence Ministry had cleared several unmanned systems under the Make category, among them SAVIOR, a semi-submersible autonomous vessel for intelligence and reconnaissance, CASCADE-ASW, an autonomous craft for anti-submarine warfare.Industry has moved since then, Sagar Defence's USV Matangi completed a 1,600km autonomous journey from Karwar to Thoothukudi in 2024, and Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers delivered the Jaldoot USV to the Naval Science and Technological Laboratory in December 2024. Bharat Electronics Limited has developed a solar-powered USV for hydrographic surveys and coastal surveillance.Operating them across India's waters is a challenge. The western coast has rougher seas, stronger swells and long monsoons, which puts heavy demands on hull design, propulsion, sensors and communications. Smaller craft must balance endurance and low observability against the need to stay afloat in difficult conditions. Communications are another requirement, since USVs need high-bandwidth links, satellite relays and resilient mesh networks that can withstand jamming, interception and cyber threats. The Navy has also identified the need for a Unified Platform Management System that can run several unmanned platforms from a single console.The focus is now shifting from individual vessels to an integrated maritime network. How well it performs will depend on reliable communications, common control systems, indigenous technology and the ability to operate in India's varied waters.

articles.title: In 1942, Army Air Corps serviceman Raymond Brim went AWOL for nearly 48 hours to marry Pat before shipping overseas; their daughter passed on Pat’s wartime letters 77 years later
articles.summary: Explore the heartfelt correspondence between Raymond and Patricia Brim during World War II, highlighting their love story that endured through separation and service. Discover the significance of their wartime letters, recently preserved and shared with historian Andrew Carroll.
articles.body: On February 14, 1944, 20-year-old Patricia Brim sent her husband, Raymond, a photograph which accompanied a letter from home. In the letter, she playfully described the pose in the picture and mentioned that she wished to continue sending him pictures so that he would never forget her. This letter was part of the exchange that documented the couple’s separation during the Second World War. Raymond Brim served with the US Army Air Corps in Europe, in which he carried out bombing missions against the Nazis.Prior to his overseas posting, Raymond had taken an extraordinary step to marry Patricia. As he was unable to obtain leave from his air base in Wyoming, he went absent without leave (AWOL) and travelled to Utah for the wedding. He was away from his post for nearly 48 hours, according to The Washington Post. A subsequent profile from the University of Utah revealed that he was away for three days as his crew covered for him.A wedding before leaving the country for overseas dutiesDuring his late teens, Raymond Brim had been studying at the University of Utah and working in a mine. The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, however, changed his plans. According to the university profile, Brim left his studies and enlisted in the Army Air Corps. After completing his training, he was awaiting assignment to join his combat group in England and fly the B-17 Flying Fortress. But before the assignment, he wanted to marry Patricia, whom he had met on a blind date.While the couple had expected a small wedding, Patricia’s former school’s headmistress, however, reportedly arranged for the entire student body of Rowland Hall in Salt Lake City to walk to St. Mark’s Episcopal Cathedral to attend the wedding in December 1942. The university’s account describes the wedding as a pit stop before Raymond’s deployment in England.Letters exchanged across the Atlantic as Raymond flew combat missionsLetters and pictures became an important way to communicate for the couple once Raymond was deployed overseas. One of Patricia’s surviving messages was written ahead of Christmas 1943, in which she recalled their previous Christmas together, including a meal, a decorated tree and attending church in the snow. She expressed that she missed him and hoped that they would be able to spend the next Christmas together.By the time Patricia sent her Valentine’s Day photograph in 1944, Raymond had already been flying missions over Europe. The University of Utah profile reports that he served with a special unit of the 482nd Bomb Group. The unit’s aircraft reportedly used the Pathfinder radar guidance system. The technology helped bomber crews navigate and identify targets when cloud cover made visibility difficult. The 482nd was formed particularly to provide radar-equipped Pathfinder aircraft for the Eighth Air Force’s bombing formations.Raymond reportedly completed 25 combat missions and received the Distinguished Flying Cross and four Air Medals. Following his final mission, he was assigned to train new pilots. His daughter, Celia Straus, recalled in an interview that her father had promised himself he would return home to Patricia. He came back to her after surviving the war, and they remained married for 65 years before Patricia died in 2007. Raymond died in 2019, as noted by The Washington Post.A daughter’s decision to pass on the lettersAfter her parents’ death, Straus inherited a folder filled with her mother’s correspondence. In February 2021, she handed her mother’s letters to historian Andrew Carroll, whom she had known for years through their work on veteran support projects.Notably, Carroll had been collecting wartime correspondence since 1989, when a family member gave him a letter written during World War II. What had begun as a single document soon expanded into a collection of more than 100,000 letters from American conflicts. With The Washington Post, he shared that letters written by women to their husbands were considered particularly valuable because servicemen were often unable to bring their wives’ correspondence home. Therefore, the survival of these letters from Patricia added a women’s perspective to the record of wartime correspondence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At two North Dakota bridge sites, pavement and weather sensors detected conditions that could produce ice and automatically triggered fixed nozzles to spray deicer; evaluations reported 50–66% fewer crashes at the treated locations
articles.summary: Discover how innovative Fixed Automated Spray Technology in North Dakota cuts bridge crash rates significantly during winter, enhancing road safety with automated de-icing solutions.
articles.body: When the weather is wintry, bridges can be treacherous, even if other roads are mostly thawed out. In 2007, North Dakota automated a new road system that helped reduce how pavement sensors and computer-controlled spray equipment can pre-empt such hazards before ice forms. Named Fixed Automated Spray Technology (FAST), the system continuously measures pavement and air temperature and dispenses anti-icing chemical in anticipation of freezing.An evaluation of two installations by researchers at North Dakota State University found that the technology cut crashes by 50% to 66% at the bridge locations where it was installed, which may offer a useful option for roads that experience repeated winter crashes. NDDOT began work on the project after finding bridges where crashes frequently occurred during winter weather. The project had two installations: one on I-29 near Buxton and another on the I-94 Red River Bridge at the North Dakota-Minnesota border near Moorhead, Minnesota. These installations showed how automated maintenance equipment could help transportation agencies react better to changing road conditions without waiting for the crew.Why bridge decks become dangerous during winterBridge decks can become icy more quickly than adjoining roads because they are exposed to cold air from both above and below, allowing their surfaces to lose heat rapidly. As a result, moisture from rain or snow can freeze on a bridge even when nearby road surfaces remain relatively safe. This difference in the surface conditions can catch motorists off guard, increasing the risk of skidding and collision. According to the evaluation of North Dakota Fixed Automated Spray Technology (FAST) systems, the Buxton and Red River bridges were selected because of their history of winter-related crashes. The Buxton Bridge system became operational in December 2002, while the Red River Bridge system began operating in 2007. This first installation covers 370 feet of roadway and bridge deck, including approximately 330 feet of bridge deck. The second one extends across 2,300 feet of roadway, of which 1,300 feet consists of bridge decking.How a sensor-based spray system prevents ice formationThe FAST installation contains pavement sensors, environmental sensor stations, and computer-controlled spray equipment. Pavement sensors provide continuous monitoring of surface temperature and moisture and can tell whether the roadway surface is dry or wet and what the freezing point of any liquid present is. The other environmental monitoring equipment provides extra data, such as temperature, dew point, wind speed, and rate of precipitation. When the data from the sensors hit a threshold indicating the potential for frost, freezing, or precipitation, the system fires a command to the spray equipment. This system fires a command to the spray equipment to dispense a liquid anti-icing solution on the bridge deck.The solution lowers the moisture’s freezing point on the surface, which can help prevent ice formation and adhesion to the pavement. Both systems use what is known as CryoTech CF7, an anti-icing solution that is made of potassium acetate. According to a 2009 study by North Dakota State University researchers Shawn Birst and Mohammad Smadi, the anti-icing solution was chosen for its low-temperature performance and reduced structural damage. The equipment also allows maintenance personnel to monitor conditions remotely and to initiate preventive measures when necessary. Research published in the Canadian Journal of Civil Engineering has highlighted the importance of reliable environmental sensors, appropriate installation locations, and regular maintenance for the successful operation of FAST systems.Crash reductions and the challenges of automated treatmentNorth Dakota’s installation results were analysed with crash data from 12 winter seasons, January 1996 to May 2008, and compared crash rates before and after the system was installed, leaving out crashes caused by things the technology could not impact, such as animals or rocks on the road. At Buxton Bridge, the average crashes per winter season decreased from 6.2 before the system was installed to 2.5 after, a 59% reduction. Adjusted for changes in average daily traffic counts, the reduction was 66% for property damage crashes, 62% for injury crashes, and 75% for fatalities.The Red River Bridge also improved, with a total drop in crashes on the North Dakota side; after traffic adjustments, crash totals dropped 55%. On the Minnesota side, they dropped overall 46%. The total on both sides dropped about 50%. The system was estimated to be at least 95% effective, though its use was limited. For example, spraying was halted when the wind speed hit 15 miles per hour because high winds could cause the mist to blow off the roadway, and the equipment was shut down when road temperature fell below 12 degrees Fahrenheit because keeping the mist effective would require much more of the chemical.Financial reviews provided an additional silver lining. At Buxton, the benefit-to-cost ratio was 4.3, while for Red River it was 1.3 over 20 years. The benefit calculation included the decreased cost of congestion and maintenance. The team showed how automated de-icing technology could complement traditional winter road maintenance, particularly at bridges that tend to attract a lot of accidents in winter.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Cuban father of a US-born child was detained by immigration officers in Kentucky for nearly six months; a November 10 federal ruling found his detention unlawful and ordered his immediate release
articles.summary: A Cuban man detained by US immigration authorities for nearly six months must be released immediately, a federal court in Kentucky ruled on Tuesday.
articles.body: A Cuban man detained by US immigration authorities for nearly six months must be released immediately, a federal court in Kentucky ruled on Tuesday. The court found that officials had failed to follow the required legal process before keeping him in custody, violating his constitutional right to due process.The ruling available on Justia, concerns Damichel Jesus Viamontes Castellano, who was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers on May 19. He had earlier been taken into custody by US Border Patrol agents in Texas in 2022 but was allowed to remain outside detention while his immigration case proceeded.Castellano has since been held at the Oldham County Detention Center in La Grange, Kentucky. His immigration case took another turn on July 28, when an immigration judge directed that he be removed to Cuba. However, he challenged that decision, and his appeal is still being considered by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA).The pending appeal was important to the court's decision because the removal order had not yet become administratively final. The judge also noted that both sides agreed that Castellano's detention fell under Section 1226(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. This provision allows immigration authorities to hold a person while deciding whether they should be removed from the country.Castellano has family and business connections in Kentucky. He is the father of a child born in Louisville in 2024 who is a US citizen. His mother is also a lawful permanent resident and has an approved family petition filed on his behalf. He runs an active Kentucky business, as its sole organiser and registered agent.According to the court, officials had not properly assessed whether he needed to remain in custody or informed him of the procedure available to challenge that decision.How ICE brought Castellano back into custodyCastellano first came to the attention of US immigration authorities in 2022, when Border Patrol agents arrested him in Texas. He was issued a notice to appear in immigration proceedings and subsequently released on his own recognisance.ICE revisited his case in May. Officers found that he had earlier received the immigration notice and had faced charges of DUI and reckless driving in February 2025. These charges prompted the agency to plan a targeted operation to take him into custody.ICE arrested him on May 19 and withdrew the release granted to him in 2022. Officials issued several immigration documents, including a warrant of arrest, but did not give him Form I-286, the notice used to communicate an initial custody decision.That missing document became central to the court proceedings. It allows a detained person to understand the government's decision and seek a review by an immigration judge, including a hearing to request release on bond.The court found no record showing that ICE had considered Castellano's individual circumstances before deciding to detain him. Under the applicable rules, officers must examine whether a person is likely to attend future immigration hearings and whether their release would create a safety risk.The judge also found that the government had not established that Castellano received the required information about his detention or how he could challenge it.Why court rejected government's argumentThe government maintained that Castellano should have approached the immigration court himself to seek a fresh decision on his custody. Its lawyers argued that he could have filed a request for a bond hearing rather than approaching the federal court directly.Castellano argued that immigration officials had failed to complete the initial steps required by their own rules and could not shift the responsibility to him after leaving those steps unfinished.The federal judge accepted this argument. The court found that the authorities had not carried out the initial custody review or provided the necessary notice. It therefore declined to make Castellano complete another administrative process before considering his challenge.The judge also considered the time he had already spent in custody. By the time he approached the court, he had remained detained for more than 120 days without an independent judicial examination of the decision to keep him there.The ruling further addressed the responsibility of proving whether detention was necessary. The government wanted the detained person to demonstrate that they were neither a danger to the community nor likely to flee.The court disagreed with this approach. It held that the government must establish through clear and convincing evidence that a person presents a danger or flight risk during a bond hearing under Section 1226(a).In explaining its position, the judge pointed to the difficulties faced by people in immigration detention. They may struggle to collect documents and evidence, understand complicated immigration procedures or obtain legal assistance. The court said these difficulties made it important for the government to justify continued detention.It also considered Castellano's earlier release. ICE had allowed him to remain outside custody after his 2022 arrest but later decided to detain him again. The court found that the government had not shown why keeping him confined without the required review was justified.ICE directed to release him immediatelyThe judge concluded that the failure to assess Castellano's case individually and inform him of his right to challenge detention had deprived him of due process under the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution.The court also considered the impact of detention on personal freedom and the government's reasons for holding him. It found that immigration authorities had not established a sufficient basis for continuing his confinement without following the prescribed safeguards.It consequently granted his petition for a writ of habeas corpus, along with his request to expedite the proceedings.The ruling also places conditions on any attempt to detain him again. Unless circumstances have materially changed, officials must first provide him with a bond hearing under Section 1226(a).You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Man pays Rs 5,760 for 6-month gym membership, alleges lights switched off 15 minutes before closing time and steam bath remained non-functional, quits within 2 months; consumer court orders gym to pay Rs 6,500
articles.summary: An Amritsar resident who paid Rs 5,760 for a six-month gym membership but quit within two months over complaints of premature closures and inadequate
articles.body: An Amritsar resident who paid Rs 5,760 for a six-month gym membership but quit within two months over complaints of premature closures and inadequate facilities has won Rs 6,500 in a consumer dispute. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Amritsar, directed M/s Oceanic Gym to refund Rs 3,500 after deducting charges for the period the customer used its facilities. It also ordered the fitness centre to pay Rs 2,000 in compensation and Rs 1,000 towards litigation expenses, besides 6% annual interest on the refund.The commission, in an order dated October 21, 2026, gave the gym 45 days to comply.Bharigu Sharma bought a six-month membership at Oceanic Gym on November 7, 2024, paying Rs 5,760. He alleged that the fitness centre had promised hygienic premises, professional trainers, safety arrangements and facilities including a steam bath.However, Sharma told the commission that the gym regularly began shutting down before its advertised closing time of 10pm. Lights and music were switched off early, while the steam bath allegedly remained out of order. He also raised concerns about equipment sanitation and the absence of adequate emergency medical assistance. Unable to continue working out there, Sharma joined another gym on January 27, 2025, paying Rs 15,000, and sought a refund from his former fitness centre. After his requests allegedly went unanswered, he approached the consumer commission.Oceanic Gym contested the complaint, saying Sharma had attended trial sessions before enrolling and had been satisfied with the facilities. It maintained that the gym remained operational until 10pm, although its winding-up routine began at 9.45pm, when the lights and music were switched off. The management said notices explaining the arrangement had been displayed on the premises.To counter the allegations about the steam bath, it produced a register and affidavits from other members. On safety concerns, the gym said its proprietor, Dr Parminder Singh Sachdeva, was a doctor and that four doctors were available throughout the day at the dental clinic on the ground floor. It also submitted photographs of its first-aid kit, safety charts and cleaning arrangements, arguing that it had fulfilled its obligations.The commission examined the membership documents, payment receipt and evidence submitted by both parties. It found that the gym's own account established that its winding-up process began 15 minutes before the advertised closing time. The bench said customers who had paid for a membership were entitled to access the essential facilities throughout the advertised operating hours. Merely displaying notices about an earlier winding-up routine did not absolve the gym of its responsibility, particularly when it had not established that Sharma had been informed of and agreed to the restriction before purchasing the membership.It also rejected the argument that Sharma's trial sessions absolved the gym of its responsibility to maintain the promised standards throughout the membership period. The commission noted that he had used the facilities for approximately two months before joining another gym. It concluded that Oceanic Gym had failed to establish that it had delivered the services promised at the time of enrolment, amounting to deficiency in service under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.The commission partly allowed Sharma's complaint and fixed the refundable amount at Rs 3,500 after accounting for the two months of membership he had used. Oceanic Gym must pay 6% annual interest on this amount from the date the complaint was filed until payment is made. It must also pay Rs 2,000 for the inconvenience caused and Rs 1,000 towards litigation expenses. The total payout comes to Rs 6,500, excluding interest. articles.title: A U.S. paratrooper and his London sweetheart lost touch after D-Day; more than 70 years later, he flew from Virginia to Australia to see her again
articles.summary: A brief romance during the Second World War came to an end when a soldier was sent overseas.
articles.body: A brief romance during the Second World War came to an end when a soldier was sent overseas. Decades later, a chance encounter and a missed taxi went in their favour as they discovered a wartime romance after more than 70 years apart. As reported by ABC News, the 93-year-old US Army veteran travelled to South Australia from his home in Virginia in February 2016 to reunite with his long-lost sweetheart, Joyce Durrant Morris.The pair met in London in 1944, when Joyce was 17 and Norwood Thomas was 21, during World War II. Their association had been cut short when he was deployed to the war front and rekindled by a series of letters, after which they lost touch. Until one of them did an internet search for their names over 70 years later. Donations and one airline helped the 93-year-old veteran make the extraordinary tripA chance meeting in London before D-DayThomas and Morris first met in London in 1944, while American troops were in Britain preparing to go to war in Nazi-occupied Europe. Thomas was a member of the US Army 101st Airborne Division, an elite paratrooper unit that would arrive in France and take part in the Normandy landing on 6th June 1944. Their meeting was quite an accident. Another serviceman in his unit had stopped at a bridge spanning the River Thames when two young women appeared. The soldiers approached them, and Thomas and Morris eventually hit it off. They spent a few months together before he was posted away.The relationship came with obvious complications. During his service, Thomas was ultimately deployed to Normandy, where Americans parachuted behind enemy lines to support the Allied invasion. He sometimes tried to make his way back to London so that he could see Morris, even if just for a few days. Unfortunately, the relationship was brief, as Thomas was called back to the US in the waning days of the war, with little time for goodbyes. Subsequently, they wrote to each other for some time, but the separation posed too much of a strain for them to bear.A misunderstanding that kept them apart for decadesBack in America, Thomas continued his correspondence with Morris and finally proposed to her to come back to America and marry him. She misinterpreted the letter and took it as Thomas having met someone else. Therefore, she refused, saying that she was becoming a nurse in Britain. The misunderstanding was left unresolved, and the letters stopped. Both married other people. Morris went to Australia with her husband, and Thomas stayed with his wife in America. Morris divorced her husband approximately 30 years after her marriage, while Thomas remained with his wife until she died in 2001.Though time had elapsed, neither had completely forgotten the relationship. Morris was said to have had a picture of Thomas and stared at it for years after the war. Thomas said that he remembered her and that she stayed in his mind long after they parted. The chance of rekindling their romance arose in 2015 when Morris showed her son a photograph of Thomas and asked him to look on the Internet. Finally, her son Robert located his name in a newspaper clipping of the D-Day landing in The Virginian-Pilot. Their chance reunion, over 70 years after they had last seen each other, commenced with a telephone call and a shared Skype video call with members of both their families. The conversation brought back memories of what they had shared.A 10,000-mile journey for a long-awaited reunionAfter years of reestablishing the relationship with Thomas, the pair finally arranged to meet face to face. At 93, Thomas was due to leave Virginia Beach and travel over 10,000 miles to Adelaide. The story of their reunion was picked up by the media around the world, and hundreds of people contributed to an online fundraising page. Air New Zealand organised a free upgrade to first class for Thomas and his son Steve, helping them make the long journey. The flight was scheduled for February 2016, with Thomas arriving at the airport on 11 February. Nervous as he was, he was happy he would be able to see the woman he remembered for most of his life.The couple’s reunion was emotional. They hugged, they kissed, and Thomas said he was glad he had finally been able to see Morris again. The meeting was covered by Australian broadcaster ABC and other news outlets. Thomas spent a couple of weeks with his former love in Adelaide on Valentine's Day, and their reunion did not erase the years they had spent apart, but it did give them a chance to revisit unfinished parts of their lives.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Friday accused the Modi government of tapping his phone, claiming that the Prime Minister was
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Friday accused the Modi government of tapping his phone, claiming that the Prime Minister was aware of the surveillance. He once again challenged PM Modi to a face-to-face public debate, saying it would expose who was under the control of foreign powers and involved in anti-national activities."The Prime Minister is aware of this because he has my phone tapped," Rahul said in a video posted by the Congress on X.Rahul also shared another video on X later, accusing PM Modi of relying on a script and claiming that the pressure of facing him in a debate was getting to the Prime Minister."The stage is yours, the atmosphere is yours—yet you still needed a script. Looks like the pressure got to you," Rahul wrote in the caption.Reiterating his challenge, the Congress leader said, "Anyway, no worries. Bring a teleprompter to a debate with me too, and seat a judge of your choice as well.""Just show up, that’s all. The country wants to know - who is the real traitor?" he added.In the video, Rahul claimed that a direct debate with him could end PM Modi's political career.Rahul said, “I kept repeating it. The Prime Minister's political career, mark my words, the PM's political career will be over if he comes and debates with me. He knows that, and I know that. He keeps calling me anti-national. I want to show the nation exactly who is anti-national, exactly who's controlled by whom and since when. And he knows the truth of that."“Notice something. There's a little fear in his mind because he's no longer commenting on me. He's no longer attacking me. He's been very, very careful. There's a reason for it, guys,” Raebareli MP said.Akhilesh backs RahulBacking INDIA bloc colleague, Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav said that phones and modern technology could not be trusted in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI)."One should not trust the technology of today. In the age of AI, anything is possible," Akhilesh said, referring to Rahul's phone-tapping allegation.He also recalled that a leader who was no longer alive had once spoken about his phone being tapped.BJP hits backMeanwhile, the BJP hit back at Rahul's allegations, with Kerala BJP chief Rajeev Chandrasekhar dismissing the phone-tapping claim and launching a personal attack on the Congress leader."Rahul Gandhi, I can only safely say to him, with all respect, must get his head examined. Nobody is bothered tapping his phone. Nobody is interested in tapping his phone. If anybody is interested, it's to understand why his brain only functions on lies day after day," Chandrasekhar said.The BJP had earlier rejected Rahul's demand for a debate with PM Modi. Union home minister Amit Shah had challenged the Congress leader to debate him in Parliament instead, asking Rahul to bring his allegations and arguments to the House rather than take the political debate to the streets.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Is chennai drying up ahead of dog days?
articles.summary: The city is running low on water, both above and below ground.
articles.body: The city is running low on water, both above and below ground. A poor monsoon so far has left reservoirs with 48% less water than they held at this time last year, while groundwater levels are about 45% deeper.Metrowater is looking to the sky for relief. “If we don’t get more rain, we might have to consider rationalising water supply, while relying on desalination plants,” an official said.The city’s five principal reservoirs, Poondi, Cholavaram, Red Hills, Chembarambakkam and Kannankottai-Thervoy Kandigai, held 4.79 thousand million cubic feet (tmcft) on Thursday, compared with 10tmcft on the same day last year. That is 41% of their combined capacity of 11.75tmcft.Groundwater levels also dipped. The average depth rose from 3.77m in Oct 2025 to 5.48m in Oct this year, a fall of 1.71m, or 45%. Madhavaram recorded the sharpest fall, from 5.80m to 10.81m. However, levels across city has improved by nearly a metre from last month.Metrowater says desalination will cushion the shortfall. On Wednesday, the 110 million litres a day (mld) and 150mld plants supplied 100mld and 87mld, respectively. By Thursday, the supply rose to more than 100mld in both plants. “Both the Nemmelli plants can be operated at full capacity. By Feb, the Minjur plant, which has a 100mld capacity, will yield at least 20mld,” a senior official said. “We are confident of handling the situation,” he said.Water experts are not so optimistic. They warn that the situation is worrying and the offered solution is dangerous. “Surplus rain was expected this year. But that has not been the case,” said S Janakarajan, a retired professor at Madras Institute of Development Studies. Evaporation from the soil and water lost through plants, together called evapotranspiration, would be very high in summer.Janakarajan said the state govt lacked a water security plan despite several warnings about El Niño. “Chennai receives an average of 120cm of rainfall every year. Desalination plants can never be solution. Govt is taking an easy way out, which harms coastal ecosystem,” he said.Sekhar Raghavan, Chennai’s ‘Rain Man’ and founder of The Rain Centre, an NGO, said residents should not wait for govt to supply water. They should recharge groundwater themselves. “By this time, Chennai should have had at least 140cm of rainfall, but we received only 110cm as of Nov 10,” he said.The govt must act on two fronts. “First, appoint third-party monitors for rainwater harvesting. In many places, builders have not constructed the systems properly, yet the CMDA approved them,” he said. TVK govt relaunched its rainwater-harvesting initiative. “But enforcement will not improve without outside monitors,” he said.“Second, govt must draw up a preventive plan, and it must involve experts with decades of experience,” he said. “The govt must change its attitude and seek external expertise.”“Both floods and droughts are man-made,” he said. “If govts do not learn from experience, the same problems will recur, and we will keep having the same discussions with no change.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: Karnataka issues order to launch menopause health programme pilot in Dakshina Kannada
articles.summary: BENGALURU: The Karnataka government has issued an order to launch a three-month pilot of its mid-life women’s health and menopause programme, ‘Ruthu
articles.body: BENGALURU: The Karnataka government has issued an order to launch a three-month pilot of its mid-life women’s health and menopause programme, ‘Ruthu Taare’, in Dakshina Kannada district, with dedicated clinics and comprehensive health screenings for women aged 35 and above.The programme, which will cover women in perimenopause, menopause and post-menopause, aims to address health concerns that often go undiagnosed or are dismissed as a normal part of ageing. It will offer screening for non-communicable diseases and cancers, mental health assessments, nutrition counselling and referral services.“Women’s health does not end with motherhood, and menopause should never be a journey women are expected to endure in silence,” said Health Minister U T Khader.According to the order issued by the Commissionerate of Health on November 12, dedicated clinic sessions will be held every Wednesday at primary health centres (PHCs), taluka hospitals and district hospitals. Saturday clinics will be organised at designated medical colleges, subject to feasibility and the availability of personnel.The screening will cover hypertension, diabetes, obesity and other cardiometabolic risk factors, apart from breast and cervical cancer screening. A Mid-Life Health Card will be developed to document screening results, clinical assessments, investigations, referrals and follow-ups.The programme will also address mental health concerns among women during mid-life. A Green-Yellow-Red risk classification system will be introduced to identify women requiring different levels of mental health support, with referral linkages to existing services, including Gruha Arogya.The order also states that nutrition counselling will focus on balanced diets, adequate protein and calcium intake, locally available nutritious foods, bone health, osteoporosis prevention and healthy weight management.District health authorities have been directed to map existing healthcare facilities, identify participating centres and assess the availability of infrastructure, personnel and specialist referral services. ASHAs, ASHA mentors, community health officers, medical officers and nursing staff will be trained to facilitate implementation.“Every woman deserves to age with dignity, live with good health and receive care at every stage of life,” Khader said.The district health officer will submit monthly progress reports. The pilot will be evaluated after three months based on screening coverage, referral completion, service availability, operational feasibility and resource requirements. Based on the findings, a proposal to refine the programme and expand it in phases across the state will be submitted, officials said.The initiative is part of Karnataka’s broader efforts to strengthen women's healthcare. The state has also been working towards a dedicated women's health policy, with an initial focus on menopause, and plans to introduce a one-year menopause fellowship to develop a specialist workforce.Actress and former MP Ramya, the ambassador for ‘Ruthu Taare’, welcomed the move on X, saying, “Menopause is finally on the public health map.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Why is Kheer known as God’s own food?
articles.summary: Indians and their love for Kheer is beyond words!
articles.body: Indians and their love for Kheer is beyond words! Kheer, also known as Payesh or Payasam, is a traditional delight that is often prepared during special festivals and occasions, so much so that this sweet treat is an inseparable part of the Indian festivals and occasions and is believed to be God’s own food and is considered pious. Here’s more to know about kheer?The traces of historyAs per Indian tradition, the history of Kheer dates back to the Ramayana era, and the mention of this dish can also be found in the epic Mahabharat. In Sanskrit the word Kheer is known as "kshira" or "kshirika," which simply means a dish made with milk and rice, which makes it God’s pwn food. This history dates back to the famous story from the Ramayana, wherein King Dasharatha wanted children, so he did a sacred fire ritual. From the fire came a divine being carrying a bowl of payasam. The king shared it among his queens and sons who were born, including Rama. So kheer is linked to a gift from the gods themselves.Offered to the Gods firstIn Hindu tradition food is first offered to the deity as "naivedyam" and then shared with everyone as "prasad." Kheer or payasam in the south is one of the common offerings. People offer it to gods during festivals like Diwali, Ganesh Chaturthi and Navratri. Some temples are famous for their kheer. At the Jagannath temple in Puri it is part of the "Mahaprasad,". The temple's cooking tradition is said to be about 2,000 years old. At the Ambalappuzha Krishna temple in Kerala the sweet paal payasam is given to pilgrims every day. A legend says Lord Krishna in disguise asked a king to serve payasam to all visitors and the temple still follows this today.What makes it so piousKheer is made with a few simple things: milk, rice, sugar or jaggery and often ghee and cardamom. In thought milk is a pure and nourishing food. Kheer is called "sattvic," which means light, clean and calm. Ayurveda also describes it as a nourishing food that builds strength. Because of this kheer is linked to the start of life. In families a babys first solid food is a spoonful of kheer in a ceremony called Annaprashana.Brings people togetherAnother reason kheer feels special is how it is shared. When a big pot of kheer is cooked and served, everyone gets a share, poor. At the Ambalappuzha temple the story is about feeding every visitor, it is believed that sharing the food is part of its meaning. North India has kheer Kerala has payasam in types Bengal has payesh and Punjab has Phirni. The rice may change to vermicelli, semolina or dal. The feeling stays the same: warmth and celebration.A quick noteKheer is rich in sugar and ghee, so enjoy it in portions, especially if you have diabetes or are watching your weight. In a nutshell, it can be concluded that Kheer earns the name "Gods food" because of its place in old stories its role in temples its simple pure ingredients, and the way it brings people together. It is a sweet that connects us to faith, family and tradition, one spoonful at a time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: A Massachusetts woman started growing mushrooms in her basement closet as a hobby; seven years later, her farm was producing around 1,000 pounds every week
articles.summary: A mushroom-growing experiment that began in a basement closet eventually developed into a commercial farming operation producing hundreds of pounds of
articles.body: A mushroom-growing experiment that began in a basement closet eventually developed into a commercial farming operation producing hundreds of pounds of mushrooms every week. Julia Coffey, founder of Mycoterra Farm in Massachusetts, began cultivating mushrooms in January 2010, initially treating it as a small hobby business. What started with limited space and modest production gradually expanded as customers showed interest in her harvests. According to an interview published by Boston Voyager, Coffey reinvested earnings into the operation, eventually moving beyond her basement to greenhouses and, later, a dedicated farming facility.How a basement closet mushroom experiment became a growing farmCoffey's journey into mushroom cultivation was shaped by earlier experience. In her interview with Boston Voyager, she explained that she had spent 4 years working at mushroom farmer Paul Stamets' farm in Washington state before returning to her hometown of Westhampton, Massachusetts, in 2009.After struggling to find fulfilling employment, she decided to start growing mushrooms in January 2010. The initial operation occupied a closet in her basement, with cultivation primarily intended as a hobby business rather than a large agricultural enterprise.The mushrooms soon found customers at local food co-operatives and farmers markets. Their reception encouraged Coffey to reinvest the money she earned, alongside income from other jobs, into expanding the farm.The early growth was gradual because mushroom-growing equipment was expensive. Rather than immediately investing in a large facility, she increased production as resources became available, allowing the business to develop at a manageable pace.Boston Voyager reported that Coffey purchased the house she was renting in December 2012, enabling her to expand the mushroom laboratory further into the basement. She also began growing mushrooms in the garage, although she later acknowledged that it had not been the best decision.What made mushroom growing suitable for a small spaceThe Fungi Academy explains why cultivation can be accessible to people without conventional farmland. A basement, garage, shed or spare bedroom can provide space for a small growing operation, while even a modest setup can produce mushrooms for household consumption.A basic mushroom-growing kit costing approximately $20 can provide two or three harvests with regular misting over around two weeks. A larger investment of roughly $100 beyond the kit could help someone establish a small urban mushroom farm capable of producing hundreds of pounds of gourmet and medicinal mushrooms.The approach does not mean that commercial farming is effortless. Coffey's experience illustrated how a small operation could become more demanding as production increased. Her initial success required her to invest not only in additional equipment but also in more suitable growing environments.Demand pushed the operation beyond its original spaceAs Mycoterra Farm attracted more customers, its original growing arrangements became increasingly difficult to maintain. Boston Voyager reported that Coffey's partner, Chris, joined the business in autumn 2013, bringing additional enthusiasm and helping her pursue further expansion.The first major expansion was completed in January 2015. The farm added an insulated container that served as a walk-in cooler, alongside two greenhouses measuring 24 by 48 feet. Insulation and radiant heating helped the greenhouses support mushroom production throughout the year.The additional space allowed Coffey to increase output, but it did not take long for the expanded operation to encounter another limitation. As production grew to fill the greenhouses, the farm was again approaching its capacity.Coffey hired three employees during 2015, while a family member who had previously helped at farmers markets also began working on the farm. The growing team enabled Mycoterra to handle a larger operation and its increasing customer demand.According to Boston Voyager, the farm eventually used pallet racks extending from the floor towards the ceiling to make the most of its greenhouse space. This arrangement helped increase production to approximately 500 pounds of mushrooms a week, although demand continued to exceed what the facility could supply.A larger facility transformed the small mushroom businessThe next significant change came when Coffey and her partner discovered a vacant building that had previously operated as an equestrian centre. Boston Voyager reported that they encountered the property while making a delivery to a local restaurant around New Year.The building offered the space required to expand beyond the greenhouses. After months of negotiations and financing challenges, Coffey purchased the property in August 2016. But converting it into a mushroom-growing facility required extensive renovation.The farm finally moved from Westhampton to South Deerfield in December 2017. Boston Voyager reported that production quickly doubled to around 1,000 pounds a week following the relocation.What mushrooms did the farm grow and sellMycoterra Farm developed a range of specialty mushrooms. In her Boston Voyager interview, Coffey listed shiitake, lion's mane, chestnut, nameko, reishi and enokitake among the mushrooms grown at the farm.The business also expanded beyond selling fresh produce. Coffey explained that Mycoterra supplied mushroom-growing spawn to other cultivators and offered kits for people interested in growing mushrooms at home. She had also developed Mycoglow, a mushroom-based skincare range featuring products such as soaps, lotions, toners, bug sprays and scrubs.Fungi Academy describes mushroom cultivation as an activity that can serve several purposes, from supplying food to supporting small businesses. It highlights the potential for home growers to produce gourmet varieties, including oyster mushrooms, shiitake and lion's mane, without requiring conventional agricultural land.For Coffey, the operation also involved maintaining the quality of the mushrooms as production increased. Boston Voyager reported that Mycoterra maintained its own culture library and produced spawn in-house, rather than relying entirely on commercial suppliers.The challenges behind expanding mushroom productionBoston Voyager reported that she identified short shelf life, a lack of familiarity with mushrooms among some consumers and the need to maintain sterile conditions during early growth as particular challenges.Coffey told Boston Voyager that she had regularly worked more than 60 hours a week for 8 years. Mushroom cultivation required continuous attention, leaving limited opportunities for time off. The new South Deerfield facility also created opportunities to reach wholesale markets while retaining sales through farmers markets and restaurants.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
